Swiss🇨🇭 12/22/2024 9:12 PM
Mood - Debatable most people feel like shit especially in the first few weeks on it. Sleep - Not necessarily the best, Keto elevates circulating corticosteroids iirc and thus can disrupt sleep. Seemed to be similar in my case when I did it. It felt like my sympathetic nervous system was pretty active most of the time. Arthritis - Sure if keto has any sort of merit it's probably for people with autoimmune conditions, it seems to have very potent anti-inflammatory effects also in my experience, so for arthritis it may make sense although there are lots of other great strategies to treat arthritis without having to do keto. Problems I've experienced and think that are counterproductive, are for instance significant weight loss especially in terms of water weight, which may make you look emaciated, it also seems to hinder athletic performance at high intensities while low at low itensities it seems to be quite similar to regular food consumption, which is likely due to less efficient glycogen replenishment during training. Your hormone profile will also be pretty fucked as your SHBG generally goes sky high on keto due to insulin suppression, although a lot of these effects are more relevant for natty's as they are much more susceptible to these effects, in people on AAS these effects won't be very noticeable as the AAS somewhat compensate the deficits. Also keto in naturals may induce hypothyroidism due to insulin's stimulating role in thyroid function. Again people that aren't natty may be less effected as AAS increase BMR and thermogenesis. If one is prone to cramping one may experience a increase in frequency as the kidney struggles to hold on to electrolytes without insulin and glucose. Thus electrolyte excretion is pretty elevated in people on keto and is also often a reason on why keto dieters quit. Also there seems to be concerning correllations of low carbohydrate dieters having a measurable increase in mortality, so you may be cutting your lifespan short.

Low-carbohydrate diets and their combination with high-protein diets have been gaining widespread popularity to control weight. In addition to weight loss, they may have favorable short-term effects on the risk factors of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Our objective was to elucidate their long-term effects on mortality and CVD incidence.
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0055030
Prospective cohort study of women and men who were followed from 1980 (women) or 1986 (men) until 2006. Low-carbohydrate diets, either animal-based (emphasizing animal sources of fat and protein) or vegetable-based (emphasizing vegetable sources of fat and protein), were computed from several validated food-frequency questionnaires assessed during follow-up.
https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/abs/10.7326/0003-4819-153-5-201009070-00003
The overall low-carbohydrate score was associated with a modest increase in overall mortality in a pooled analysis (hazard ratio [HR] comparing extreme deciles, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01 to 1.24]; P for trend = 0.136). The animal low-carbohydrate score was associated with higher all-cause mortality (pooled HR comparing extreme deciles, 1.23 [CI, 1.11 to 1.37]; P for trend = 0.051), cardiovascular mortality (corresponding HR, 1.14 [CI, 1.01 to 1.29]; P for trend = 0.029), and cancer mortality (corresponding HR, 1.28 [CI, 1.02 to 1.60]; P for trend = 0.089). In contrast, a higher vegetable low-carbohydrate score was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR, 0.80 [CI, 0.75 to 0.85]; P for trend ≤ 0.001) and cardiovascular mortality (HR, 0.77 [CI, 0.68 to 0.87]; P for trend < 0.001).
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261561420304787

8:57 PM
Adrenoceptors presently are classified into three main subclasses: alpha1-, alpha2-, and beta-receptors, each with three (perhaps more) subtypes. All three alpha1-adrenoceptor subtypes are present in rat brain. The purpose of this review is to assess the role of alpha1-adrenoceptors in the modulation of synaptic transmission and plasticity, as well as their ability to modulate higher cerebral functions, such as attentional and memory processes. However, since there are no truly subtype-specific agonists or antagonists available at present, it is virtually impossible to allocate a particular central effect to one or other of the subtypes. The activation of alpha1-adrenoceptors reduces the firing probability and glutamate release in the cornu ammonis of the hippocampus. Alpha1-Adrenoceptors may flexibly modulate weak and strong activation of the pyramidal neurones in the neocortex. Alpha1-Adrenoceptors play only a minor role in the modulation of long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, and may influence many brain functions also via non-neuronal mechanisms. since glial cells can express alpha1-adrenoceptors. At the behavioural level, the activation of alpha1-adrenoceptors promotes vigilance and influences working memory and behavioural activation, while having only a minor role in the modulation of long-term memory.

JC Denton 2/25/2025 6:17 AM
It's very complex and nuanced. The cognitive enhancement is likely from catecholamine and histamine release in the PFC, striatum, and hippocampus. TAAR1 activation and VMAT2 reversal mediates this release. It sensitizes D1, but inhibits D2. Likely increases D-serine, acetylcholine, enkephalin, and BDNF release via D1. Chronically it upregulates Glua1 via PKA/CREB, downregulates mglur2, and potentiates NR2B. Increases glutamate levels via EAAT3 internalization. Also carbonic anhydrase inhibition. (edited)

“Studies have demonstrated that dopamine and dopaminergic systems in the midbrain play a key role in OCD; specifically, patients experience an activation of D1 receptors. Studies in rodents have found a decrease in excessively stereotyped grooming or “OCD-like” activities when D1 receptors have been knocked out (Berridge and Aldridge, 2000; Zike et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2022). Additionally, this has been determined by receptor binding research using radioisotopes; evidence indicates that dopamine transporter binding ability is compromised in OCD, specifically in subcortical areas of the putamen and caudate (van der Wee et al., 2004; Koo et al., 2010). Overall, studies have shown that monotherapy with SSRIs in treating OCD may not fully treat patients, and many patients benefit from the addition of an antipsychotic medication that displays a dopaminergic mechanism of action due to the interaction of serotonin and dopamine (Korsgaard et al., 1985; Koo et al., 2010).”
